title: Amex Roofing
description: An English and Chinese website for a Bay Area roofing contractor, with inspection requests, calendar integration, and clear recovery when a requested time is unavailable.
highlights: Generated English and Chinese pages from shared content and maintained a common booking flow across both languages.

homepageSummary: An English and Chinese website that turns a homeowner’s inspection request into a scheduling workflow for a Bay Area roofing contractor.

caseStudy.summary: I built a bilingual website and inspection-request workflow for a Bay Area roofing contractor, connecting the public form to serverless scheduling routes and making failure states part of the interface.

sections.title: Make the next step clear
paragraphs: A homeowner arrives with a roof problem and needs a practical next step: call the contractor or request an inspection. The site puts those choices beside the service explanation. The booking flow collects a property address, contact details, preferred date, and one-hour arrival window. Its receipt says “Inspection requested” and explains that the crew will call to confirm. That distinction keeps a successful form submission from promising a completed appointment.
My work covers the public interface, the bilingual page structure, and the serverless booking integration. This is client delivery, separate from the independent products elsewhere in my portfolio.

figure.alt: Amex Roofing inspection-request receipt showing a fictional address and preferred arrival window.
figure.caption: Sample inspection receipt with a simulated success response.

sections.title: Keep both languages on one workflow
paragraphs: English and Chinese pages use a shared visual system and booking behavior. Build scripts generate the translated homepage and service-area pages from maintained source content. That keeps layout and interaction changes from turning into two unrelated implementations. The language choice also travels with the inspection request, giving the crew useful context for the follow-up.

The front end uses HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, while provider credentials stay in serverless routes. A form can still submit through its native POST path when the enhanced browser flow is unavailable. The tradeoff is maintaining consistent validation and messages across both the browser and server.

sections.title: Validate before touching the calendar
paragraphs: The booking route checks the request source and validates contact, address, date, and time fields before delivery. The browser shows errors near the field that needs attention. Date selection and availability requests also need to handle responses arriving out of order: changing the selected date must not let an older response overwrite the current choice.

Local booking-contract checks exercised rejected origins, invalid inputs, accepted date windows, and the native-form fallback. Separate calendar-sync checks confirmed that a failed notification does not advance the synchronization checkpoint. Holding that checkpoint until delivery succeeds gives a later retry a chance to recover the missed notification.

sections.title: Recover when a time is taken
paragraphs: An available slot can become unavailable between selection and submission. The interface handles the server’s conflict response by clearing the selected time, marking busy windows unavailable, and placing an explanation beside the time field. The address and contact fields remain populated so the user can choose another window without starting over.

A controlled browser check reproduced this sequence with a simulated slot-conflict response. The deployed interface kept the contact information, cleared the unavailable time, and moved attention to the field that needed correction. This makes recovery part of the normal form flow.

figure.alt: Amex Roofing booking form preserves sample contact information and asks the user to choose another arrival window after a simulated conflict.
figure.caption: Simulated slot conflict: contact details stay in place while the user chooses another arrival window.

sections.title: Delivered scope and remaining limits
paragraphs: The delivered site joins service information, bilingual content, and an inspection-request flow in one customer-facing experience. The important boundary is between receiving a request and completing the crew’s scheduling process. The public receipt reflects that distinction, while the integration handles validation and delivery behind it.

The next engineering step is to exercise the complete scheduling lifecycle in a controlled environment, including duplicate requests, delayed provider responses, and notification retries. Those checks would extend the existing contracts from individual boundaries to the whole workflow.

caseStudy.evidenceNote: Screenshots use the deployed UI with fictional inputs and simulated API responses. Local contract checks used mocked dependencies; no bookings were sent. Captured September 5, 2026.

highlights: Streamed debounced code snapshots over a WebRTC data channel alongside realtime audio, with structured interviewer briefs kept on the server.

caseStudy.context: Independent product · Realtime voice and code · 2025–present
caseStudy.summary: I built a mock-interview workspace that connects spoken reasoning with the candidate’s code. The engineering work centers on editor synchronization, temporary session credentials, and a session lifecycle that ends visibly and cleans up resources.

sections.title: Give the interviewer the code context
paragraphs: Practicing a coding interview means explaining an approach while writing and revising code. A voice-only interviewer misses those changes; a text-only workflow loses the spoken explanation. SoloMock places a Monaco editor beside the problem and transcript, and sends editor snapshots through the same WebRTC connection used for the conversation.

The example shows a candidate explaining a hash-map solution to Two Sum, including why a lookup happens before insertion. Keeping the solution and transcript together lets the candidate review both the implementation and the reasoning used to explain it.

figure.alt: SoloMock displays a completed Python Two Sum solution beside a sample spoken explanation and interviewer follow-up.
figure.caption: Sample code and transcript in a simulated interview session.

sections.title: Send useful changes, not every keystroke
paragraphs: The editor waits for a pause before sending a snapshot and skips unchanged code. The current implementation uses a 2.5-second debounce. This reduces repetitive context updates while still letting a revised solution enter the conversation. The tradeoff is deliberate delay: this mechanism is not a promise that the model sees each keystroke immediately.

Problem content is structured separately from the transport. Interviewer briefs hold solution approaches, hint ladders, follow-ups, and edge cases; the browser receives the candidate-facing problem. That gives the interview a consistent source of context while keeping the editor and WebRTC code focused on interaction.

sections.title: Treat the session as a lifecycle
paragraphs: The browser requests microphone access before asking the server for a temporary credential. The long-lived provider key remains on the server. Once connected, the client manages the audio tracks, data channel, countdown, and transcript. Explicit stop, timeout, and lost connection all lead into cleanup instead of leaving an apparently active interview behind.

There are important limits to these safeguards. The duration timer runs in the client. Rate limiting uses a shared Redis service when configured, but falls back to per-instance memory when that service is unavailable. These controls reduce exposure; they do not establish an unbypassable session boundary or a hard total spending cap.

sections.title: Make a lost connection understandable
paragraphs: A connection can fail after the user has already invested time in an answer. The interface ends the session, explains that the connection was lost, and offers a way to start again. It retains the transcript and code so the user can still review the work and request post-session feedback.

In a controlled connection-loss check, changing a mocked WebRTC peer to failed triggered the cleanup path: the audio track stopped, the peer closed, and the error appeared. The feedback component then accepted a simulated response while keeping the interview work available for review.

figure.alt: SoloMock shows a lost-connection message, retained code and transcript, and a feedback card populated from a test fixture.
figure.caption: Simulated connection loss with retained interview work and sample feedback.

sections.title: What the checks establish
paragraphs: Local tests cover the problem-brief structure, rate-limiter behavior, and session-route response. The browser demonstration also exercised editor snapshot delivery and cleanup through substituted dependencies. These checks concentrate on the boundaries that connect the interface, transport, and server.

The next evaluation should focus on the interviewer itself: a declared set of practice sessions, consistent assessment criteria, and observed response behavior. Application correctness and useful coaching are different questions. The session and feedback structure gives that evaluation a repeatable starting point.

caseStudy.evidenceNote: Screenshots use the deployed UI with sample code, transcripts, and simulated media and provider responses. Connection cleanup was checked with mocks; no paid session was started. Captured September 5, 2026.

contribution: I projected map geometry on the server and separated snapshot delivery, caching, and interactive comparisons.

caseStudy.context: Independent product · Maps and data delivery · 2026
caseStudy.summary: I built a fuel-price map and comparison toolkit around published price snapshots. The application separates server-side map geometry, dated data delivery, and browser interactions such as state selection and trip-cost calculation.

sections.title: Connect the map to a useful question
paragraphs: A national map gives a quick comparison, but a visitor may want to inspect one state or estimate fuel for a trip. Gasolytics connects the overview to state and metro details, price history, a trip calculator, and EV comparisons. The map’s selected state opens a panel with the corresponding prices and trend instead of sending the reader through a separate search.

The capture shows California selected with a visible snapshot date. The panel connects its map position to prices and history, so a reader can move from a national pattern to a specific place. State and metro averages describe an area, rather than individual station quotes.

figure.alt: Gasolytics map with California selected, metro price pins, a dated state price, and a price-history panel.
figure.caption: California selected with dated price data and a state trend. Captured September 5, 2026.

sections.title: Project the geometry on the server
paragraphs: The server uses d3-geo to turn geographic shapes into SVG path strings. The browser receives those shapes and handles the interactive layer: selection, zoom, pan, and metro pins. This keeps map projection separate from the changing price data and from the event-handling code.

Changing a fuel grade updates the displayed prices without rebuilding the geographic projection in the browser. The geometry is imported as a traced asset instead of read from an assumed runtime file location, so the serverless deployment includes the shapes it needs. The tradeoff is sending rendered paths with the page rather than making the browser compute them.

sections.title: Keep the snapshot date distinct
paragraphs: The separate Databank project publishes AAA snapshots; Gasolytics reads them from Vercel Blob. It does not perform the upstream scraping in the request path. The application shapes the snapshots for its views and uses a short-lived, in-process cache so repeated reads can reuse a result.

The response carries both the source data date and the time it was read. Those have different meanings: a page can be rendered now from an older snapshot. The current cache lasts up to 30 minutes within a process, while page revalidation and the upstream publication schedule are separate concerns. A recent request alone does not prove fresh source data.

sections.title: Explain both estimates and unavailable data
paragraphs: The trip calculator exposes the assumptions behind its result: distance, fuel economy, selected fuel grade, and the state averages used for price. Visitors can enter their own distance instead of relying on the approximate city-to-city distance. The result is a planning estimate, with the method beside it, rather than an unexplained dollar amount.

Unavailable data needs a separate response. I tested the data reader against local synthetic snapshots with network access disabled. A successful read populated the cache; an expired cache followed by an unreadable input returned the previous result marked stale. A fresh process without usable data raised an explicit error instead of returning an invented price.

figure.alt: Gasolytics trip calculator displays selected cities, fuel economy, the average price used, and a calculated fuel-cost estimate.
figure.caption: Trip estimate with its distance, fuel economy, and price assumptions. Captured September 5, 2026.

sections.title: What this demonstrates and what comes next
paragraphs: The work connects a published data artifact to an interactive comparison: read and shape the data, render stable geometry, expose useful detail, and explain the estimate. The local checks establish the tested cache and failure behaviors, while the public interface makes the underlying date and calculation inputs visible.

The next improvement I would validate is how clearly readers distinguish fresh, cached, and unavailable data across every view. The same status should mean the same thing on the map, detail pages, and calculators, with the actual source date available wherever it affects a decision.

caseStudy.evidenceNote: Public map and calculator captured read-only on September 5, 2026. Cache and failure checks used isolated local fixtures with network access disabled.

title: Plugrade
description: Trust index for Claude Code plugins: security audits with file-and-line evidence, plus a daily record of what the official directory ships and how installs move.
highlights: Built the daily snapshotter (Playwright on GitHub Actions) that records install counts for 300+ plugins from claude.com/plugins into a Neon Postgres time series. It has run every day since July 31, 2026

Made the scrape refuse bad data. A run only commits if row counts stay in bounds, nearly every row has a count, yesterday's slugs are still present, and no count drops more than 20% in a day. A failed gate keeps the last good snapshot and opens an issue
Wrote the audit publishing pipeline with a default-deny embargo, so an unpublished finding can never be reached by URL. A test pins the rule and fails if the old default comes back
